name: Premchand
line: Village India, money and dignity, told in plain Hindustani with a moral sting.
signature: Premchand writes ordinary people (farmers, children, widows, clerks) caught between need and self-respect. The narrator talks to you like an elder, comments on the characters, and lets irony do the hurting. Big emotion arrives through small objects: a pair of tongs, a shroud, a blanket.

techniques.name: The small object that carries the theme
techniques.how: Hang the whole story on one cheap, concrete thing (Hamid's chimta) and let every character react to it.

techniques.name: Narrator as a warm commentator
techniques.how: The narrator steps in with a line of judgement or wit, then steps back into the scene.

techniques.name: Lists of everyday detail
techniques.how: Open with a rush of village activity (buttons, shoes, oxen) to put us inside the day before the plot starts.

techniques.name: Child's-eye logic
techniques.how: Let a child argue like a lawyer; his innocent reasoning exposes the adults' world.

excerpts.text: रमज़ान के पूरे तीस रोज़ के बाद आज ईद आई है। कितना मनोहर; कितना सुहावना प्रभात है। वृक्षों पर कुछ अजीब हरियाली है, खेतों में कुछ अजीब रौनक है, आसमान पर कुछ अजीब लालिमा है। आज का सूर्य देखो, कितना प्यारा, कितना शीतल है, मानों संसार को ईद की बधाई दे रहा है। गाँव में कितनी हलचल है। ईदगाह जाने की तैयारियाँ हो रही हैं। किसी के कुरते में बटन नहीं है। पड़ोस के घर से सुई-तागा लेने दौड़ा जा रहा है। किसी के जूते कड़े हो गये हैं, उनमें तेल डालने के लिए तेली के घर भागा जाता है। जल्दी-जल्दी बैलों की सानी-पानी दे दें। ईदगाह से लौटते-लौटते दोपहर हो जायेगा। तीन कोस का पैदल रास्ता, फिर सैकड़ों आदमियों से मिलना-भेंटना। दोपहर के पहले लौटना असम्भव है। लड़के सबसे ज़्यादा प्रसन्न हैं। किसी ने एक रोज़ा रखा है, वह भी दोपहर तक, किसी ने वह भी नहीं है लेकिन ईदगाह जाने की खुशी उनके हिस्से की चीज़ हैं। रोज़े बड़े-बूढ़े के लिए होंगे। इनके लिए तो ईद है।
excerpts.note: A rush of tiny village details (a missing button, stiff shoes, oxen to feed) puts us inside Eid morning before any plot. Notice the narrator's asides: 'रोज़े बड़े-बूढ़े के लिए होंगे। इनके लिए तो ईद है।'

excerpts.text:
दोनों खेत की दशा देख रहे थे। मुन्नी के मुख पर उदासी छाई थी; पर हल्कू प्रसन्न था।
मुन्नी ने चिंतित होकर कहा --- अब मजूरी करके मालगुजारी भरनी पड़ेगी।
हल्कू ने प्रसन्न-मुख से कहा --- रात की ठण्ड में यहां सोना तो न पड़ेगा।
excerpts.note: The ironic ending: the crop is destroyed, the wife despairs, and Halku is happy because he won't have to sleep in the cold field again. One line of dialogue reverses the whole story's meaning.

name: Jaishankar Prasad
line: Lyrical, Sanskrit-rich prose of history, romance and sacrifice.
signature: A Chhayavaad poet writing prose: long musical sentences, nature as a mirror of feeling, and heroes and heroines torn between love and duty, often against a historical backdrop. Endings are usually renunciation, not victory.

techniques.name: Landscape as emotion
techniques.how: Describe sea, night or lamp-light so it tells us what the character feels before they speak.

techniques.name: Love against duty
techniques.how: Put the lovers on opposite sides of a loyalty (nation, family, vow) so the choice costs something.

techniques.name: Elevated diction
techniques.how: Choose tatsam words and rhythmic phrasing for a heightened, poetic register.

excerpts.text:
"बन्दी!"
"क्या है? सोने दो।"
"मुक्त होना चाहते हो?"
"अभी नहीं, निद्रा खुलने पर, चुप रहो।"
"फिर अवसर न मिलेगा।"
"बड़ा शीत है, कहीं से एक कम्बल डालकर कोई शीत से मुक्त करता।"
"आँधी की सम्भावना है। यही अवसर है। आज मेरे बन्धन शिथिल हैं।"
"तो क्या तुम भी बन्दी हो?"
"हाँ, धीरे बोलो, इस नाव पर केवल दस नाविक और प्रहरी हैं।"
"शस्त्र मिलेगा?"
"मिल जाएगा। पोत से सम्बद्ध रज्जु काट सकोगे?"
"हाँ।"
excerpts.source: Jaishankar Prasad ki Shreshth Kahaniyan, Hindi Wikisource
excerpts.note: The story opens in pure dialogue, in the dark: two prisoners, no names, no description. Tension first, landscape later. When the storm arrives, it mirrors their escape.

name: Saadat Hasan Manto
line: Partition, sex workers, madness: told flatly, ending with a shock.
signature: Manto writes like a reporter at a crime scene: short sentences, no sermon, no tears. He goes where polite literature won't (riots, brothels, asylums) and ends on one devastating line or image that flips everything before it.

techniques.name: The last-line punch
techniques.how: Build quietly, then end on one line or gesture that reveals the true horror or irony.

techniques.name: Clinical tone for terrible events
techniques.how: Describe violence plainly; the reader supplies the emotion.

techniques.name: Compassion for the outcast
techniques.how: Give the 'immoral' character the most human moment in the story.

name: Ismat Chughtai
line: Bold, funny, intimate stories of women inside middle-class Muslim homes.
signature: Chughtai writes in the chatty, idiomatic speech of women at home: gossip, teasing, taunts. Under the comedy are desire, loneliness and power within the family. A child or young girl often narrates what she half understands.

techniques.name: Begumati zubaan
techniques.how: Use women's household idiom, proverbs and taunts as the music of the prose.

techniques.name: The half-understanding narrator
techniques.how: A child narrates; the reader understands more than she does.

techniques.name: Comedy hiding pain
techniques.how: Keep the surface funny so the dark truth lands harder.

name: Harishankar Parsai
line: Hindi satire (vyangya): deadpan, short and merciless about hypocrisy.
signature: Parsai takes an absurd premise (a policeman sent to the moon, a dead man's soul stuck in government files) and narrates it with a straight face. Every sentence carries a jab at bureaucracy, politics or religion.

techniques.name: Absurd premise, serious tone
techniques.how: State something impossible as plain fact and follow its logic to the end.

techniques.name: Bureaucratic language as a weapon
techniques.how: Let officials speak in jargon that exposes their emptiness.

techniques.name: One target per piece
techniques.how: Pick one hypocrisy and hit it from every angle.

name: Phanishwar Nath Renu
line: Regional (aanchalik) fiction full of folk song, dialect and sound.
signature: Renu makes a region, rural Purnia in Bihar, the hero. His pages are full of sounds, folk songs, local words and festivals. Plot is loose; atmosphere and community carry the story.

techniques.name: Sound on the page
techniques.how: Write the dhol, bells and calls as words, so the reader hears the village.

techniques.name: Folk song as commentary
techniques.how: Drop in a song whose lines comment on the scene.

techniques.name: Dialect as character
techniques.how: Let each character's local speech show class and place.

name: Mannu Bhandari
line: Quiet, sharp stories of modern marriages and women's choices.
signature: Bhandari writes urban middle-class women deciding between two men, a career and a family, honesty and comfort. The prose is plain, the drama inward, and the endings often leave the choice uncomfortably open.

techniques.name: Diary-like interiority
techniques.how: Let the heroine's thoughts contradict what she says aloud.

techniques.name: The undramatic crisis
techniques.how: Make a phone call or a letter the turning point, not a fight.

techniques.name: Open ending
techniques.how: Stop at the moment of choice and let the reader decide.

name: Nirmal Verma
line: Lyrical, inward prose of memory, silence and loneliness.
signature: Verma's stories happen mostly inside people: in pauses, in rooms at dusk, in what they don't say. Hill stations and European cities, fog and rain; long sentences that drift like memory.

techniques.name: Silence as dialogue
techniques.how: Let the most important line go unsaid; write the pause around it.

techniques.name: Weather as mood
techniques.how: Fog, rain and dusk set the emotional key of the scene.

techniques.name: Memory folding into the present
techniques.how: Slide between now and then without a hard break.

name: Salim–Javed
line: The angry young man, mythic plots and dialogue that becomes a proverb.
signature: Salim Khan and Javed Akhtar built larger-than-life heroes with a wound (a tattooed insult, a murdered father), a clear enemy and a moral choice. Every big line is set up earlier, so when it comes it lands like thunder. Mother, brother, and law versus loyalty are the engines.

techniques.name: Setup and payoff dialogue
techniques.how: Plant a phrase or object early; pay it off in the climax with a twist in meaning.

techniques.name: The hero's wound
techniques.how: Show the childhood injustice in the first minutes; everything after is the hero answering it.

techniques.name: Two brothers, two paths
techniques.how: Split one moral question between two characters who love each other.

techniques.name: The quotable line
techniques.how: Short, rhythmic, a contrast in two halves, built on character, not decoration.

name: Gulzar
line: Poet-filmmaker: everyday images made strange, relationships told softly.
signature: Gulzar joins senses that don't usually go together (a fragrance you can see, a voice you can touch) and finds poetry in small household things. His films are about relationships breaking and mending, often told out of order through memory.

techniques.name: Synaesthetic image
techniques.how: Describe one sense with another to make a familiar feeling new.

techniques.name: Non-linear memory
techniques.how: Tell a relationship through flashbacks triggered by objects or places.

techniques.name: Restraint in dialogue
techniques.how: Characters say less than they feel; one soft line carries the scene.

name: Hrishikesh Mukherjee
line: Warm middle-class comedies and dramas about decent people.
signature: Mukherjee's films (written with collaborators like Gulzar and Rajinder Singh Bedi) find drama in everyday middle-class life: a job interview, a new cook, a dying friend. Comedy comes from character and misunderstanding, never cruelty.

techniques.name: Comedy of deception
techniques.how: One small lie snowballs; the fun is watching it be maintained.

techniques.name: The outsider who heals a house
techniques.how: A newcomer (cook, patient, guest) quietly fixes a broken family.

techniques.name: Gentle stakes
techniques.how: Keep the stakes human-sized so warmth, not spectacle, drives the story.

name: Anurag Kashyap
line: Gritty small-town crime, dark humour and raw Hindi.
signature: Kashyap's stories are messy and alive: gangs, obsession, revenge across generations, told with street dialogue, sudden violence and dark jokes. Structure often breaks into chapters or jumps in time.

techniques.name: Violence with a joke beside it
techniques.how: Put an absurd or funny beat right next to brutality to unsettle the audience.

techniques.name: Dialect and swearing as truth
techniques.how: Let characters speak exactly as they would in their town.

techniques.name: Generational revenge
techniques.how: Spread one feud across fathers and sons so history drives the plot.

name: Juhi Chaturvedi
line: Slice-of-life family stories with quiet, specific humour.
signature: Chaturvedi finds stories in topics nobody films (sperm donation, constipation, a comatose co-worker, an old landlord) and plays them through family bickering and small rituals. Low plot, high texture; feeling arrives sideways.

techniques.name: The unglamorous premise
techniques.how: Build a film on an everyday or awkward subject people really live with.

techniques.name: Family argument as music
techniques.how: Overlapping, repetitive bickering that reveals love.

techniques.name: Emotion through routine
techniques.how: Show change through a habit that shifts (a morning walk, a tea order).

name: Varun Grover
line: Poetic realism, satire and the small towns of North India.
signature: A lyricist and satirist, Grover writes characters trapped by caste, family or exams who reach for dignity. Banaras ghats, coaching cities, poetry inside working-class lives; humour that cuts.

techniques.name: Poetry in ordinary mouths
techniques.how: Give a working-class character a line of real poetry that changes the scene.

techniques.name: System as antagonist
techniques.how: Let caste, exams or the law be the real villain, not one person.

techniques.name: Satire without a sermon
techniques.how: Make the absurdity visible and let the audience judge.

name: Vishal Bhardwaj
line: Shakespeare in the Indian hinterland, with dialect and music.
signature: Bhardwaj moves classic tragedies into Mumbai's underworld, UP's badlands and Kashmir, keeping the structure and changing the soul. Earthy dialects, black humour, songs that do plot work.

techniques.name: Classic structure, local skin
techniques.how: Keep a proven plot skeleton; rebuild every detail from a real Indian place.

techniques.name: Dialect as world-building
techniques.how: Characters' speech (Khari Boli, Kashmiri-Urdu) tells us where we are.

techniques.name: Songs that move plot
techniques.how: A song should change a relationship, not pause the story.

name: Sriram Raghavan
line: Noir thrillers with twists, dark comedy and film-buff homage.
signature: Raghavan builds thrillers where one wrong decision spirals: crime that goes wrong, revenge that rots, liars cornered. Twists are fair (clues are on screen), and dark comedy keeps tension crackling.

techniques.name: The decision that spirals
techniques.how: One choice early on traps the hero in consequences that keep multiplying.

techniques.name: Fair-play twist
techniques.how: Show every clue on screen; the twist reframes what we already saw.

techniques.name: Comedy inside suspense
techniques.how: Let an absurd interruption stretch the tension of a dangerous scene.

name: Anton Chekhov
line: Ordinary lives, precise details, endings that stay open.
signature: Chekhov watches people without judging them. He picks a few exact details (a beret, a white dog, a slice of watermelon) and lets them carry character. Stories end not with resolution but with the realisation that the hardest part is just beginning.

techniques.name: The telling detail
techniques.how: Choose one or two specific, slightly odd details instead of a full description.

techniques.name: No villain, no verdict
techniques.how: Show people as they are; let the reader judge, or not.

techniques.name: The open ending
techniques.how: End at a moment of understanding, not of resolution.

techniques.name: Chekhov's gun
techniques.how: Anything you show prominently must matter later; cut what doesn't.

excerpts.text:
It was said that a new person had appeared on the sea-front: a lady with a little dog. Dmitri Dmitritch Gurov, who had by then been a fortnight at Yalta, and so was fairly at home there, had begun to take an interest in new arrivals. Sitting in Verney's pavilion, he saw, walking on the sea-front, a fair-haired young lady of medium height, wearing a beret; a white Pomeranian dog was running behind her.

And afterwards he met her in the public gardens and in the square several times a day. She was walking alone, always wearing the same beret, and always with the same white dog; no one knew who she was, and every one called her simply "the lady with the dog."

"If she is here alone without a husband or friends, it wouldn't be amiss to make her acquaintance," Gurov reflected.
excerpts.source: The Tales of Chekhov, vol. 3, tr. Constance Garnett (1917), English Wikisource
excerpts.note: Three details make her a person: a beret, a white Pomeranian, always alone. Gurov's cynical thought in one line gives us his whole character.

excerpts.text:
Then they spent a long while taking counsel together, talked of how to avoid the necessity for secrecy, for deception, for living in different towns and not seeing each other for long at a time. How could they be free from this intolerable bondage?

"How? How?" he asked, clutching his head. "How?"

And it seemed as though in a little while the solution would be found, and then a new and splendid life would begin; and it was clear to both of them that they had still a long, long road before them, and that the most complicated and difficult part of it was only just beginning.
excerpts.source: The Tales of Chekhov, vol. 3, tr. Constance Garnett (1917), English Wikisource
excerpts.note: The famous open ending: no solution, only the realisation that 'the most complicated and difficult part of it was only just beginning.'

name: O. Henry
line: City stories with a playful narrator and a twist ending.
signature: O. Henry's narrator chats with the reader, makes jokes and long, showy words, then springs an ironic twist in the last lines that turns the story into a parable.

techniques.name: The twist ending
techniques.how: Plant the twist's ingredients openly; reveal how they combine only at the end.

techniques.name: A narrator with personality
techniques.how: Let the narrator joke and comment like a storyteller at a tea stall.

techniques.name: A precise money detail
techniques.how: Ground the story in an exact, small sum or price.

excerpts.text: ONE dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all. And sixty cents of it was in pennies. Pennies saved one and two at a time by bulldozing the grocer and the vegetable man and the butcher until one’s cheeks burned with the silent imputation of parsimony that such close dealing implied. Three times Della counted it. One dollar and eighty-seven cents. And the next day would be Christmas.
excerpts.source: The Four Million (A. L. Burt), English Wikisource
excerpts.note: An exact sum, repeated, as the first line and the last but one. The money detail is the whole conflict, stated before we know who Della is.

excerpts.text: The magi, as you know, were wise men—wonderfully wise men—who brought gifts to the Babe in the manger. They invented the art of giving Christmas presents. Being wise, their gifts were no doubt wise ones, possibly bearing the privilege of exchange in case of duplication. And here I have lamely related to you the uneventful chronicle of two foolish children in a flat who most unwisely sacrificed for each other the greatest treasures of their house. But in a last word to the wise of these days let it be said that of all who give gifts these two were the wisest. Of all who give and receive gifts, such as they are wisest. Everywhere they are wisest. They are the magi.
excerpts.source: The Four Million (A. L. Burt), English Wikisource
excerpts.note: After the twist, the chatty narrator steps forward and turns the story into a parable: 'They are the magi.'

name: Rabindranath Tagore
line: Tender, humane stories of bonds across class and distance.
signature: Tagore's short stories, translated into English in his lifetime, find deep feeling in unlikely friendships (a little girl and an Afghan fruit-seller) and in the cost of social rules. A gentle narrator, often a father or observer, and endings that ache rather than shock.

techniques.name: Friendship across worlds
techniques.how: Pair two people separated by age, class or country, and let their bond grow through small rituals.

techniques.name: The observer narrator
techniques.how: A father or neighbour watches and understands slowly, with us.

techniques.name: Ending in quiet sacrifice
techniques.how: Resolve with a small, costly generous act rather than a dramatic event.

excerpts.text:
My five years' old daughter Mini cannot live without chattering. I really believe that in all her life she has not wasted a minute in silence. Her mother is often vexed at this, and would stop her prattle, but I would not. To see Mini quiet is unnatural, and I cannot bear it long. And so my own talk with her is always lively.

One morning, for instance, when I was in the midst of the seventeenth chapter of my new novel, my little Mini stole into the room, and putting her hand into mine, said: "Father! Ramdayal the door-keeper calls a crow a krow! He doesn't know anything, does he?"
excerpts.source: The Hungry Stones and Other Stories (1916), tr. Sister Nivedita, English Wikisource
excerpts.note: Character through speech: Mini is introduced by her chatter, and the father-narrator by his indulgence and his unfinished novel.

excerpts.text:
The marriage-pipes sounded, and the mild autumn sun streamed round us. But Rahmun sat in the little Calcutta lane, and saw before him the barren mountains of Afghanistan.

I took out a bank-note, and gave it to him, saying: "Go back to your own daughter, Rahmun, in your own country, and may the happiness of your meeting bring good fortune to my child!"

Having made this present, I had to curtail some of the festivities. I could not have the electric lights I had intended, nor the military band, and the ladies of the house were despondent at it. But to me the wedding feast was all the brighter for the thought that in a distant land a long-lost father met again with his only child.
excerpts.source: The Hungry Stones and Other Stories (1916), tr. Sister Nivedita, English Wikisource
excerpts.note: A quiet, costly gift resolves the story. The image of the barren mountains inside a Calcutta wedding lane holds both fathers' longing.

name: Ernest Hemingway
line: Short, plain sentences; the real story under the surface.
signature: Hemingway's 'iceberg' method: show only a little of what is going on and leave the rest underwater. Simple words, repeated phrases, dialogue where people talk around the real subject.

techniques.name: The iceberg
techniques.how: Know everything about the situation, write a fraction, and trust the reader to feel the rest.

techniques.name: Dialogue around the subject
techniques.how: Characters never name the real problem; they argue about drinks and hills.

techniques.name: Plain declarative rhythm
techniques.how: Short sentences joined with 'and'; few adjectives.

works: The Old Man and the Sea

name: Gabriel García Márquez
line: Magical realism: wonders told as plain fact, time folding on itself.
signature: Márquez narrates miracles and plagues with the calm of a grandmother telling family history. Opening lines jump across time; long, rolling sentences mix the absurd, the tragic and the funny.

techniques.name: The marvellous stated flatly
techniques.how: Describe an impossible event in the same tone as breakfast.

techniques.name: Time-folding first line
techniques.how: Open with a future moment that looks back to a past one.

techniques.name: Family as a town's history
techniques.how: Let one family's generations stand for a nation.

works: A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings

name: Raymond Carver
line: Minimalist stories of working-class couples, endings left hanging.
signature: Carver strips scenes to kitchen-table talk, drinks and silences. Nothing seems to happen, yet a marriage or a life shifts. Endings stop abruptly, leaving the reader inside the tension.

techniques.name: Kitchen-table scene
techniques.how: Put two or three people at a table and let talk reveal a crisis.

techniques.name: Cut, cut, cut
techniques.how: Remove every sentence that explains; keep only what we can see and hear.

techniques.name: The hanging ending
techniques.how: Stop just after the turn, before anyone reacts.

works: What We Talk About When We Talk About Love

name: William Shakespeare
line: Soliloquy, poetry under pressure, comedy beside tragedy.
signature: Shakespeare lets characters think aloud in verse, turning private doubt into public drama. Plots braid a main and a sub-plot; clowns and gravediggers comment on kings. Images (poison, gardens, sleep) repeat across a play to build meaning.

techniques.name: The soliloquy
techniques.how: Let a character alone on stage argue with themselves; the audience becomes their confidant.

techniques.name: Comic relief that cuts deep
techniques.how: Put a joking low-life character in the darkest scene; his jokes carry the truth.

techniques.name: Image patterns
techniques.how: Repeat one image family across the play so it gathers meaning.

excerpts.text:
To be, or not to be: that is the question:
Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer
The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune,
Or to take arms against a sea of troubles,
And by opposing end them? To die: to sleep;
No more; and, by a sleep to say we end
The heart-ache and the thousand natural shocks
That flesh is heir to, 'tis a consummation
Devoutly to be wish'd. To die, to sleep;
To sleep: perchance to dream: ay, there's the rub;
For in that sleep of death what dreams may come
When we have shuffled off this mortal coil,
Must give us pause. There's the respect
That makes calamity of so long life;
excerpts.note: A soliloquy is an argument with yourself: question, option one, option two, a complication ('ay, there's the rub'). Notice how 'to die, to sleep' repeats and turns.

name: Henrik Ibsen
line: Realist drama: a respectable home, a hidden secret, a reckoning.
signature: Ibsen sets plays in ordinary drawing rooms where a secret from the past (a forged signature, a disease, a lie) slowly comes out. Each act tightens the screw; the climax is a conversation, not a fight.

techniques.name: The past breaking into the present
techniques.how: Build the plot on a secret already done before the play begins.

techniques.name: The confrontation scene
techniques.how: Sit two characters down and let them finally say everything.

techniques.name: The door that closes
techniques.how: End on one decisive action that changes a life.

excerpts.text:
HELMER
Nora—can I never be anything more than a stranger to you?

NORA
[taking her bag] Ah, Torvald, the most wonderful thing of all would have to happen.

HELMER
Tell me what that would be!

NORA
Both you and I would have to be so changed that—. Oh, Torvald, I don't believe any longer in wonderful things happening.

HELMER
But I will believe in it. Tell me! So changed that—?

NORA
That our life together would be a real wedlock. Goodbye. [She goes out through the hall.]

HELMER
[sinks down on a chair at the door and buries his face in his hands] Nora! Nora! [Looks round, and rises.] Empty. She is gone. [A hope flashes across his mind.] The most wonderful thing of all—?

[The sound of a door shutting is heard from below.]
excerpts.source: English Wikisource (translator not named there; public-domain translation)
excerpts.note: The climax is a conversation and then a sound. Nora's refusals get shorter and shorter; the slammed door does what no speech could.

name: Vijay Tendulkar
line: Marathi theatre of power, cruelty and hypocrisy.
signature: Tendulkar exposes violence hidden in respectable society: a mock trial that turns into a real hunt, a power-hungry official, a man who 'keeps' women. Games and rituals on stage turn into cruelty.

techniques.name: The game that turns real
techniques.how: Start with play-acting or a mock event that slowly becomes an actual trial or attack.

techniques.name: Hypocrisy under a polite surface
techniques.how: Let respectable characters reveal brutality through small remarks.

techniques.name: Chorus and folk form
techniques.how: Use a chorus or folk performance style to comment on power.

name: Mohan Rakesh
line: Modern Hindi drama of incomplete people and broken homes.
signature: Rakesh writes lonely characters who want more than life gives: an artist who leaves his village love, a family where everyone is 'half complete'. Long silences, interrupted speech and one room that traps everyone.

techniques.name: Broken-off speech
techniques.how: Characters start sentences they can't finish; the gaps hold the feeling.

techniques.name: One trapping room
techniques.how: Keep the whole play in one space so pressure builds.

techniques.name: Desire for completeness
techniques.how: Every character wants something the others can't give.

name: Habib Tanvir
line: Folk theatre: Chhattisgarhi Nacha, songs and village actors.
signature: Tanvir built plays with folk performers from Chhattisgarh, using their songs, improvisation and direct address to the audience. Stories are fables with sharp political edges, and comedy carries the message.

techniques.name: Direct address
techniques.how: Characters talk to the audience, sing commentary and break the fourth wall.

techniques.name: Fable with a sting
techniques.how: A simple folk tale whose moral turns against the powerful.

techniques.name: Songs as structure
techniques.how: Songs open, link and close scenes.

name: Badal Sircar
line: Third Theatre: no stage, no sets, actors among the audience.
signature: Sircar left the proscenium for open spaces, bodies and voices only. His plays are about the trapped urban middle class, repeating patterns and the search for meaning, staged so close that the audience is part of the scene.

techniques.name: The body as set
techniques.how: Actors become walls, trains and crowds; no props needed.

techniques.name: Repetition as theme
techniques.how: Repeat the same scene with small changes to show a life stuck in a loop.

techniques.name: Audience inside the play
techniques.how: Stage it in the round so spectators are witnesses.

name: Girish Karnad
line: Myth and history retold to ask modern questions.
signature: Karnad takes a myth, folktale or historical king and uses it to ask about identity, power and desire today. He borrows folk forms (Yakshagana, a narrator-Bhagavata, masks) and mixes the comic with the tragic.

techniques.name: Old story, new question
techniques.how: Retell a known myth or history so it asks something urgent now.

techniques.name: The Bhagavata narrator
techniques.how: A narrator figure introduces, comments on and even enters the play.

techniques.name: Masks and doubles
techniques.how: Swap heads, bodies or identities to dramatise a split self.

name: Harold Pinter
line: Menace, pauses and power games in ordinary rooms.
signature: Pinter's characters fight for territory with small talk. Threat comes from what is not said; famous pauses and silences shift power. In Betrayal he tells an affair backwards.

techniques.name: The pause
techniques.how: Write silences as beats where power changes hands.

techniques.name: Menace from the ordinary
techniques.how: A stranger's polite questions become a threat.

techniques.name: Reverse chronology
techniques.how: Tell the story backwards so the audience watches innocence return.

name: Aristotle, Poetics
line: The first book on story: plot as soul, reversal and recognition.
signature: The oldest surviving study of drama. Aristotle argues that plot (the arrangement of events) matters more than character, that a story needs a beginning, middle and end bound by probability, and that the strongest moments are a reversal of fortune and a recognition.

techniques.name: Plot is the soul
techniques.how: Arrange events so each follows from the last by probability or necessity.

techniques.name: Reversal (peripeteia)
techniques.how: An action meant to help produces the opposite result.

techniques.name: Recognition (anagnorisis)
techniques.how: A character moves from ignorance to knowledge, ideally at the moment of reversal.

techniques.name: Pity and fear
techniques.how: A good-but-flawed person falling through an error moves us most.

excerpts.work: Poetics, part VI: the definition of tragedy
excerpts.text: Tragedy, then, is an imitation of an action that is serious, complete, and of a certain magnitude; in language embellished with each kind of artistic ornament, the several kinds being found in separate parts of the play; in the form of action, not of narrative; through pity and fear effecting the proper purgation of these emotions.
excerpts.source: The Poetics, tr. S. H. Butcher, English Wikisource
excerpts.note: 'Action, not narrative': drama shows, it doesn't tell. 'Complete' means a real beginning, middle and end.

excerpts.work: Poetics, part VI: plot as the soul
excerpts.text: The plot, then, is the first principle, and, as it were, the soul of a tragedy; Character holds the second place. A similar fact is seen in painting. The most beautiful colors, laid on confusedly, will not give as much pleasure as the chalk outline of a portrait. Thus Tragedy is the imitation of an action, and of the agents mainly with a view to the action.
excerpts.source: The Poetics, tr. S. H. Butcher, English Wikisource
excerpts.note: Aristotle's chalk-outline comparison: a clear plot shape matters more than beautiful details laid on confusedly.

excerpts.work: Poetics, part XI: reversal and recognition
excerpts.text:
Reversal of the Situation is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite, subject always to our rule of probability or necessity. Thus in the Oedipus, the messenger comes to cheer Oedipus and free him from his alarms about his mother, but by revealing who he is, he produces the opposite effect.

Recognition, as the name indicates, is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between the persons destined by the poet for good or bad fortune The best form of recognition is coincident with a Reversal of the Situation, as in the Oedipus.
excerpts.source: The Poetics, tr. S. H. Butcher, English Wikisource
excerpts.note: The messenger means to comfort Oedipus and destroys him: the purest reversal. Best of all when the recognition arrives at that same moment.

name: Bharata, Natyashastra
line: Indian theory of rasa: the audience tastes emotion through bhava.
signature: The Sanskrit treatise on performance. Its core idea: a performance creates rasa (an aesthetic 'flavour' such as shringara, karuna, vira, hasya) in the audience, built from the actor's bhava (emotion), its causes (vibhava), its expressions (anubhava) and passing feelings (vyabhichari bhava). Original Sanskrit is ancient; English translations here are cited by idea.

techniques.name: Pick the dominant rasa
techniques.how: Decide which rasa the scene should leave the audience tasting; make every element serve it.

techniques.name: Vibhava → anubhava
techniques.how: Show the cause of the emotion, then its outward signs (tears, trembling), not a statement of it.

techniques.name: Passing feelings
techniques.how: Layer brief contrary moods (doubt, shame, hope) over the main emotion to make it real.

name: Gustav Freytag, Technique of the Drama
line: The pyramid: exposition, rise, climax, fall, catastrophe.
signature: Freytag analysed five-act tragedies and drew drama as a pyramid: introduction, rising action, climax, falling action and catastrophe, with an 'exciting force' that starts the rise. Cited here by idea.

techniques.name: The exciting force
techniques.how: One event early on starts the conflict moving.

techniques.name: Climax in the middle
techniques.how: In tragedy, the peak of the hero's power comes mid-play; the rest is the fall.

techniques.name: The force of the last suspense
techniques.how: Just before the catastrophe, offer a glimmer of escape.

works: Die Technik des Dramas (1863), translated by E. J. MacEwan (1895)

name: Syd Field, Screenplay
line: Three acts and two plot points: the 'paradigm'.
signature: Field's paradigm: Act I setup (about a quarter), Act II confrontation (half), Act III resolution (a quarter), turned by Plot Point I and Plot Point II, events that hook into the story and spin it in a new direction. Cited by idea.

techniques.name: Plot Point I
techniques.how: Around the end of Act I, an event locks the hero into the story's conflict.

techniques.name: The midpoint
techniques.how: A central event that splits Act II and raises the stakes.

techniques.name: Plot Point II
techniques.how: The event that launches the final act and the resolution.

name: Robert McKee, Story
line: Scenes turn on values; the gap between expectation and result.
signature: McKee: every scene should turn a value (love/hate, safe/danger) from positive to negative or the reverse. A character acts expecting one result, the world answers differently, and that gap creates story. Cited by idea.

techniques.name: The turning scene
techniques.how: Name the value at stake; make sure it changes by the end of the scene, or cut the scene.

techniques.name: The gap
techniques.how: The character expects A, gets B; the next action must be bigger.

techniques.name: Controlling idea
techniques.how: State the story's meaning in one sentence: value + cause.

works: Story: Substance, Structure, Style and the Principles of Screenwriting

name: Blake Snyder, Save the Cat!
line: A 15-beat sheet and a likeable hero.
signature: Snyder's beat sheet maps a film into 15 beats (Opening Image, Theme Stated, Catalyst, Break into Two, Midpoint, All Is Lost, Finale, and more) and recommends a 'save the cat' moment that makes us like the hero early. Cited by idea.

techniques.name: Save the cat
techniques.how: Early on, let the hero do one kind or brave act so we root for them.

techniques.name: Catalyst
techniques.how: Something happens to the hero that knocks their life off course.

techniques.name: All is lost
techniques.how: Near the end of Act II, the hero loses what mattered most; hint at a 'whiff of death'.

works: Save the Cat! The Last Book on Screenwriting You'll Ever Need

name: Lajos Egri, The Art of Dramatic Writing
line: Start from a premise; build characters in three dimensions.
signature: Egri argues every play needs a premise (for example 'great love defies even death') and characters built from physiology, sociology and psychology, orchestrated so opposites clash. Cited by idea.

techniques.name: The premise
techniques.how: Write the story's argument in one line: character + conflict + conclusion.

techniques.name: Three-dimensional character
techniques.how: Define body, social world and inner psychology; they explain every choice.

techniques.name: Orchestration
techniques.how: Cast characters who are sharply different so conflict is built in.

name: Alexander Mackendrick, On Film-making
line: The director's grammar: show, don't say; build scenes from cause and effect.
signature: Mackendrick, director of The Ladykillers and Sweet Smell of Success, taught at CalArts that cinema works below words. A film should be understandable with the sound off: tell the story through what characters do and see, not what they say. He stresses cause and effect between shots, the audience anticipating what will happen next, dramatic irony, and dialogue as action rather than explanation. Cited by idea.

techniques.name: Sound-off test
techniques.how: Could the audience follow the scene with no dialogue? If not, move the story into behaviour, objects and looks.

techniques.name: Dialogue as action
techniques.how: Every line should be a character doing something to another (pleading, trapping, testing), never information for the audience.

techniques.name: Anticipation and dramatic irony
techniques.how: Let the audience know something the character doesn't, so they lean forward waiting for it to land.

techniques.name: Cause and effect between shots
techniques.how: Each shot or beat should prompt a question the next one answers.

works: On Film-making: An Introduction to the Craft of the Director (ed. Paul Cronin)

name: John Yorke, Into the Woods
line: Five-act shape, the midpoint, and change as the heart of every story.
signature: Yorke, who ran drama at the BBC and Channel 4, argues that all stories share one shape: a character with a flaw goes 'into the woods' and comes out changed. He maps it as five acts with a midpoint where the protagonist gets what they want or learns the truth, and shows the same shape repeating at the level of the act, the scene and even the beat. Want versus need, and the fractal structure of scenes, are his key tools. Cited by idea.

techniques.name: Into the woods
techniques.how: Send the hero from a known world into an unknown one that forces them to face their flaw.

techniques.name: The midpoint
techniques.how: At the centre, the hero gets what they want or discovers the truth, and the story turns.

techniques.name: Want versus need
techniques.how: Give the hero a conscious want; let the story reveal the deeper need that contradicts it.

techniques.name: Fractal scenes
techniques.how: Each scene should have its own set-up, turn and change, the whole story's shape in miniature.

works: Into the Woods: How Stories Work and Why We Tell Them

name: Konstantin Stanislavski, An Actor Prepares
line: Given circumstances, objectives and the 'magic if'.
signature: Stanislavski's system asks the actor (and the writer) what the character wants in each moment (the objective), what stands in the way, under what given circumstances, and 'what would I do if…'. Under the lines runs subtext. Cited by idea.

techniques.name: Objective in every scene
techniques.how: Give each character a playable want ('to make her stay'), not a feeling.

techniques.name: Given circumstances
techniques.how: Fix who, where, when and what just happened before the scene starts.

techniques.name: Subtext
techniques.how: Write lines that say one thing while the character wants another.

name: Uta Hagen, Respect for Acting
line: Real behaviour, substitution and the questions an actor asks.
signature: Hagen teaches actors to find truthful behaviour by asking: who am I, what are my circumstances, what do I want, what's in my way, what do I do to get it. Writers can use the same questions to test every scene. Cited by idea.

techniques.name: The actor's questions
techniques.how: Who, where, when, what do I want, what's in my way, how do I get it: answer them for each character.

techniques.name: Substitution
techniques.how: Use a real memory as the source of a character's emotion, to make the reaction specific.

techniques.name: Physical destination
techniques.how: Give characters a task with their hands while they talk.

name: Michael Chekhov, To the Actor
line: Psychological gesture and atmosphere.
signature: Michael Chekhov (Anton's nephew) gave actors the psychological gesture, one strong physical movement that captures a character's inner drive, and the idea that each scene has an atmosphere the actors must play with or against. Cited by idea.

techniques.name: Psychological gesture
techniques.how: Find one physical action that sums up the character (grasping, pushing away).

techniques.name: Atmosphere
techniques.how: Decide the scene's air (dread, celebration) and let a character fight it.

works: To the Actor: On the Technique of Acting

name: Sidney Lumet, Making Movies
line: First decide what the movie is about; every choice follows.
signature: Lumet's practical account of directing: once you know what the story is really about (its theme, not its plot), that answer decides casting, lenses, light and pace. Cited by idea.

techniques.name: What is it about?
techniques.how: Write the theme in one line and test every scene against it.

techniques.name: Visual progression
techniques.how: Change lenses or light gradually across the film to match the theme (rooms closing in).

name: David Mamet, On Directing Film
line: Tell the story in cuts of simple, uninflected images.
signature: Mamet: the director's job is to tell the story through a juxtaposition of plain shots, each one only showing what it must. Ask what the protagonist wants, and what each scene's beat is. Cited by idea.

techniques.name: Uninflected images
techniques.how: Each shot shows one simple thing; meaning comes from the cut.

techniques.name: What does the hero want?
techniques.how: State the protagonist's want for every scene; cut what doesn't serve it.

name: Walter Murch, In the Blink of an Eye
line: Editing: emotion first, the 'rule of six'.
signature: Murch ranks the reasons to cut: emotion first (by far), then story, rhythm, eye-trace and spatial rules. Writers can use it to judge where scenes should start and end. Cited by idea.

techniques.name: Emotion first
techniques.how: Cut a scene where the feeling peaks, even if information is incomplete.

techniques.name: Late in, early out
techniques.how: Enter a scene as late as possible and leave as early as possible.

works: In the Blink of an Eye

name: Sergei Eisenstein, Film Form
line: Montage: two shots colliding create a third meaning.
signature: Eisenstein argued that meaning in film comes from the collision of shots: put two images side by side and the audience makes an idea neither contains. Cited by idea.

techniques.name: Collision montage
techniques.how: Cut between two unrelated images so the audience draws a conclusion (a feast, a hungry child).

techniques.name: Rhythmic montage
techniques.how: Shorten shots as tension rises.

name: Peter Brook, The Empty Space
line: Deadly, holy, rough and immediate theatre.
signature: Brook: any empty space can be a stage if someone walks across it while someone else watches. He names four theatres (deadly, holy, rough and immediate) and pushes for theatre that's alive tonight, not dutiful. Cited by idea.

techniques.name: The empty space
techniques.how: Strip the scene to actors and audience; add only what's essential.

techniques.name: Rough theatre
techniques.how: Use popular, noisy, funny forms to reach truth.
